label: Normal Forms
notes: This appendix asks a simple question with a deep answer: how far can we simplify a vector field near an equilibrium by changing coordinates? We will peel nonlinear terms away order by order, discover that resonances among eigenvalues block some terms, and meet the Poincare and Birkhoff normal form theorems that organize the whole story.

label: The Problem Setup
notes: We center the equilibrium at the origin and split the field into its linear part, governed by the matrix and its eigenvalues, plus higher order corrections. The goal is to make a near-identity polynomial change of variables that removes as much of the nonlinear tail as possible, leaving the simplest field equivalent to the original.

label: Near-Identity Transformations
notes: The transformations we allow are identity plus a homogeneous polynomial of some degree. Such a map perturbs only terms of that degree and higher, so it never disturbs lower orders already cleaned. This triangular property is what lets us normalize one degree at a time without ever undoing earlier work.

label: The Homological Equation
notes: Substituting a degree-r change of variables turns the demand to kill the degree-r terms into a linear equation involving the bracket of the linear field with the generator. This is the homological equation. Solvability hinges on whether the linear operator it defines is invertible on the space of degree-r vector monomials.

label: Resonances
notes: On vector monomials the homological operator acts diagonally with eigenvalues given by the dot product of the exponent vector with the eigenvalues minus a single eigenvalue. When that combination vanishes the monomial is resonant and cannot be removed. The resonance condition is the exact obstruction to further simplification.

label: Resonance Diagram
notes: Plotting the eigenvalues in the complex plane lets us read resonances geometrically. A resonant relation says one eigenvalue is an integer combination of the others with nonnegative coefficients summing to at least two. We mark which lattice combinations land back on an eigenvalue, since exactly those monomials survive normalization.

label: Poincare Theorem
notes: If the eigenvalues are nonresonant, every homological equation is solvable, so all nonlinear terms can be removed formally. The Poincare theorem states that a nonresonant field is formally equivalent to its linear part. In the Poincare domain, where eigenvalues avoid the imaginary axis on one side, this linearization actually converges and is analytic.

label: Poincare-Dulac Theorem
notes: When resonances are present we cannot fully linearize, but we can remove everything except resonant monomials. The Poincare-Dulac theorem reduces the field to a normal form containing only resonant terms. This resonant skeleton commutes with the linear flow and captures the genuinely nonlinear behavior that no coordinate change can erase.

label: Small Denominators
notes: Even without exact resonance the denominators in the homological solution can be arbitrarily small, since integer combinations of eigenvalues approach an eigenvalue closely. These small denominators can make the formal series diverge. Convergence then requires Diophantine conditions bounding how fast the combinations approach resonance, the heart of the analytic theory.

label: Hamiltonian Birkhoff Normal Form
notes: For Hamiltonian systems we change variables by canonical transformations generated by a function, so the symplectic structure is preserved. Birkhoff normal form simplifies the Hamiltonian itself rather than the field, removing nonresonant terms and leaving a series in the action variables. Near an elliptic equilibrium this organizes the local dynamics into nearly integrable layers.

label: Worked Resonance
notes: We take a two-dimensional saddle with eigenvalues in ratio one to minus two and find the single resonant monomial it forces. The example shows concretely which term cannot be removed and why the normal form keeps exactly that quadratic coupling while every other quadratic term is transformed away cleanly.

label: Recap
notes: We normalize a field near equilibrium by successive near-identity changes, each solving a homological equation whose obstruction is resonance among eigenvalues. Nonresonant fields linearize formally by Poincare; resonant ones reduce to a resonant normal form by Poincare-Dulac; convergence is governed by small denominators; and Hamiltonian systems specialize to Birkhoff normal form.
